description: Burn Calendar team. I’m a software developer from Argentina. For Space Apps 2026 I took on CONAE’s challenge, Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots.
summary:
Burn Calendar is a web application that turns 25 years of NASA FIRMS fire hotspots for Argentina into one consistent record and shows it as a burning-activity calendar for any area and dates the user chooses.

MODIS has observed fires since 2000 but is being retired. VIIRS continues the record in more detail and reports about 3 times more hotspots for the same fires, so joining them as they are invents a fire boom in 2012. We convert VIIRS into MODIS-equivalent hotspots with regional day/night factors learned while both satellites flew together. Hiding one year at a time cuts the monthly error from 225% to 7.5%. Independent checks against burned area and CONAE’s own catalogue show no jump at the switch.

Users can see which months usually burn, which years were exceptional and whether this month is unusual. Every number carries an 80% uncertainty range, and users can switch harmonization off or re-test it themselves. Hotspots, series and charts are downloadable. As MODIS shuts down, this keeps the 25-year baseline usable for emergency managers, firefighters and scientists.
details:
WHAT IT DOES
Burn Calendar turns 25 years of NASA FIRMS fire hotspots for Argentina (November 2000 to October 2026) into one consistent record and shows it as a burning-activity calendar.

Users can:

  • Choose an area by drawing it on a map, picking an example area, or typing coordinates, and choose a date range.
  • Read a calendar with years in rows and months in columns, colored by hotspot count or by comparison with a normal month (the 2003–2022 median of the same month).
  • See key figures: total hotspots, this month against normal and its rank since 2001, the usual fire season, the most active year, and the busiest months.
  • Switch harmonization off to see the false jump in 2012, or hide a year (2012–2021) and test the conversion themselves.
  • Download the raw hotspots (CSV), the harmonized monthly series with uncertainty ranges (CSV), and every chart (PNG).

HOW IT WORKS
MODIS has observed fires since 2000 but is being retired. VIIRS continues the record with more detail and reports about 3.2 times more hotspots for the same fires, so joining the two as they are invents a fire boom in 2012.

A Python pipeline:

  1. Cleans the hotspots. It keeps confident detections of vegetation fires and removes volcanoes, industrial sources and offshore points.
  2. Counts hotspots on a 0.1° grid by month and by day or night pass.
  3. Learns MODIS-to-VIIRS conversion factors for each 2° region, day and night, from 2012–2021, when both satellites flew together.
  4. Converts VIIRS into MODIS-equivalent hotspots and joins the eras.
  5. Fills real satellite outages of 3 or more days and flags them in the calendar.

HOW WE KNOW IT WORKS

  • Hide-one-year test: we hid each year, learned the factors from the others and predicted the hidden year. The monthly error drops from 225% without harmonization to 7.5%.
  • Independent check against burned area (MODIS MCD64A1): at the 2012 switch, hotspots per hectare change by 0.86× in the harmonized series and by 0.84× in MODIS itself. Without harmonization the change would be 2.79×.
  • Independent check against CONAE’s own MODIS catalogue: the harmonized series stays level across the switch (0.98×). We also found that CONAE’s catalogue holds far fewer Aqua hotspots than FIRMS from 2024, which is worth reporting to CONAE.
  • Sensitivity analysis: changing the region size or the calibration weight moves the error by about one point or less.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

  • A fire baseline that survives the end of MODIS, so future VIIRS years can still be compared with 25 years of history.
  • Emergency managers and fire brigades can see when an area usually burns and whether the current month is unusual. For example, August 2026 ran at only 20% of a normal August nationwide.
  • The calendar recovers known disasters at a glance: Paraná Delta in 2008 and 2020 (August 2020 was 31 times a normal August), the Cholila fire in Patagonia in 2015, and Corrientes in 2022.
  • Every number traces back to public NASA data and open code.

CREATIVITY

  • Honest numbers: every converted value shows an 80% uncertainty range, and the calendar hatches months that could still be normal.
  • The harmonization can be switched off and re-tested live in the browser, so users do not have to take it on trust.
  • “Normal” is the median, not the average, so a few catastrophic years do not distort it.
  • It is a static website with no server, and it works on phones.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

  • The end-of-mission orbit drift of Terra and Aqua.
  • Satellite outages, and empty days that are real days without fire.
  • Day and night detection differences.
  • Small areas are noisy, so we show uncertainty ranges.
  • Recent near-real-time data may still be reprocessed.
  • What hotspots cannot tell you, listed on the page: they measure activity, not burned area; clouds hide fires; wildfires and agricultural burns are mixed.
  • Accessible colors.

TOOLS
Python (pandas, NumPy), JavaScript, D3, Leaflet, Leaflet.draw, GitHub Pages, NASA FIRMS data and API, and Claude (an AI assistant) for coding help.
